source.title: Unifying Variables in Neural Scaling for General Audio Representations via Embedding Effective Rank
source.authors: Xu-Yao Deng; Yan-Jie Sun; Yong Dou; Ke-Le Xu

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some numerical results are available only in figures; the text does not give their underlying data or fitted coefficients.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling-law analysis to general audio representations, using RankMe and HEAR downstream scores rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The study directly measures RankMe and HEAR outcomes across data, model-size, compute, masking, and architecture settings. It does not report results on language-model held-out loss, small-run prediction of much larger language-model runs, or a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its early-RankMe-to-later-HEAR correlations are included as findings about prediction by a different proxy, not as tests of V6.
record.test_reason: The study fits power-law-plus-constant laws of downstream audio quality (HEAR linear-probe score) against data volume, parameter count, compute, and joint N×D for masked-autoencoder audio models. This is a new modality bearing on V5. It reports no pretraining-loss scaling; the MSE validation loss is used only to check convergence.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that embedding effective rank unifies diverse variables, including hard-to-formalise ones such as masking rate and architecture, into a power-law relation with HEAR quality. They also report conventional power-law-plus-constant laws for data, model size and compute, each with a ceiling Q∞<1 and diminishing returns. They propose RankMe as a label-free guide for audio model scaling and selection.
record.recipe_differences: This is an audio representation study using masked-autoencoding pretraining, embedding effective rank, and HEAR downstream evaluations. It does not reproduce language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling or the original language-model compute-optimal allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted RankMe-to-HEAR parameters differ between converged and compute-constrained checkpoint sets, and across downstream tasks. Masking-rate effects on HEAR are described as non-monotonic.

fits_no_version.finding: RankMe (embedding effective rank) rises with data, model size and compute. HEAR score follows a power law in RankMe across masking rates, architectures and checkpoints, and the fitted parameters differ by checkpoint set and task.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Embedding effective rank is a unifying power-law predictor of downstream audio representation quality.

fits_no_version.finding: Early-training RankMe correlates with HEAR at 700k steps across 45 models (PCC 0.636 at 50k steps to 0.862 at 300k).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early effective rank predicts later audio representation quality.

fits_no_version.finding: In audio MAE, models with similar parameter counts give markedly different HEAR scores depending on depth and width (Section IV-D, Fig. 4a). This is an audio downstream analogue bearing against shape-insensitivity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In audio MAE encoders, architecture shape at fixed parameter count substantially affects downstream quality.

fits_no_version.finding: Base-to-Large HEAR gains differ widely by architecture: Wav2Vec2 0.539 to 0.618, HuBERT 0.677 to 0.689, Dasheng 0.794 to 0.801 (Table V).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scale gains in downstream audio quality depend on pretraining architecture.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing
record.problems: Most sweep values and fitted coefficients are presented in figures without numerical data in the text; the paper reports no uncertainty intervals for these scaling fits. Evaluation is limited to its audio models and selected HEAR scene-based tasks.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separately quantified results bearing on the listed claim versions were left out. Figure 7 architecture-specific trends are described, but no per-configuration values beyond the paired Base/Large comparisons in Table V are stated in text or tabular form.

untested.parts: No language models. No held-out pretraining loss scaling is reported.
No extrapolation from small fits to much larger runs.
There is no fitted compute-optimal N/D allocation. The study only states qualitatively that larger models reach a given HEAR score with fewer operations.
There is no language-model loss at fixed N. The audio shape effects on downstream score are noted under fits_no_version.
Language-model downstream tasks and prediction from pretraining loss are not studied. Audio downstream scaling is treated under V5.
Sensitivity of N/D/C exponent fits to setup or fitting method is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: All scaling fits are figure only, with no coefficients or uncertainty. The study is not an original source. V6 links were removed because the rows concern audio rather than language models; a curator who reads V6 as modality-general could re-add R2, R4, R6 and R8 with the same states. The reader's earlier V5 limits_scope label cited R16, which concerns the RankMe-to-HEAR relation rather than scale, so it was dropped.

versions.untested_parts: No language models or held-out pretraining cross-entropy losses are measured.
No prediction of substantially larger language-model runs from smaller-run loss fits is tested.
The study does not find a loss-minimizing parameter/token split at fixed compute or fit parameter and token growth against compute.
Architecture comparisons concern audio representation and HEAR scores, not language-model held-out loss at fixed parameter count.

Tests audio representation learning, including masking and multiple audio pretraining architectures; it does not test image/video modalities, repeated-data language-model scaling, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling laws in the specified language-model loss sense.
Tests audio downstream HEAR scores against data volume, model size, and compute. It does not test language-model downstream tasks or prediction from pretraining loss.

Reports fitting and task/architecture dependence for audio RankMe-to-HEAR relationships, but does not test language-model loss exponents, parameter-count conventions, compute-optimal splits, or departures from a single language-model loss power law.

rows.subject: en768-12
rows.operation_detail: Varied masking rate and measured HEAR average score.
rows.note: The text describes the HEAR trend across masking rates as non-monotonic and analytically intractable; it does not provide the plotted values.
rows.check: Masking rate is not a scale variable (parameters, data or compute). The non-monotonic HEAR trend does not bear on any version.

rows.subject: en768-12
rows.operation_detail: Varied pretraining data volume and measured downstream performance.
rows.note: The text reports a consistent power-law relationship between data volume and audio representation quality, with diminishing returns beyond a threshold; it says performance converges once training data exceeds approximately 2,000 hours.
rows.check: The HEAR-vs-data fit is power law plus constant, with Q∞<1. Performance converges beyond about 2,000 h of the 55 h to 277k h range, so clean power-law behaviour spans only about 1.5 orders of magnitude. The measure is downstream score, not held-out loss. Dropped V6 because this is audio, not the language-model system V6 concerns; it is better captured under V5.

rows.subject: en768-12
rows.operation_detail: Varied pretraining data volume and measured embedding effective rank.
rows.note: The text says RankMe and HEAR grow with increasing data volume with near-identical trends; plotted RankMe values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: RankMe (embedding effective rank) is a related construct, neither loss nor task performance. See fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Dasheng model series
rows.operation_detail: Varied encoder model size and measured downstream performance.
rows.note: The text reports a power-law relationship with parameter count and says performance saturates for models exceeding 100M parameters under this data setting, with diminishing returns.
rows.check: The HEAR-vs-N power law saturates above about 100M parameters at 10,666 h of data, over a narrow range of 27M to 707M. Similar parameter counts give markedly different scores. Dropped V6, as for R2.

relationships.condition: Audio MAE (Dasheng) pretraining, HEAR average score vs compute and joint model size × data
relationships.reason: HEAR follows a power-law-plus-constant compute frontier (R6), and the joint N–D law fits with a data bottleneck (R8). Values are figure only, with no uncertainty.
relationships.display_finding: HEAR scores followed a power-law-plus-constant compute frontier, while a joint model-size and data law captured a data bottleneck without reported uncertainty.

relationships.condition: Audio MAE, HEAR vs data volume and vs parameter count, measured on downstream score rather than loss
relationships.reason: Power law plus constant with Q∞<1. Data gains converge beyond about 2,000 h (R2), and parameter gains saturate above about 100M (R4), so clean scaling spans only about 1.5 orders of magnitude.
relationships.display_finding: An offset power law fitted downstream scores with Q∞<1, while gains saturated beyond about 2,000 hours and 100M parameters, leaving about 1.5 orders of magnitude of clean scaling.
